title: Build a URL-shortener service core
statement:
Step 12 · Service design

The service core maps a long URL to a stable short code and resolves codes back to URLs. This exercise fixes an in-memory, single-process contract so you can test behavior before designing the distributed system.

Build it

Process POST(url) and GET(code), returning one response per request. First-seen URLs receive base-62 sequential IDs starting at 1 with alphabet 0–9, a–z, A–Z. Repeated URLs reuse their code; unknown codes return None. Valid requests use only POST/GET and nonempty strings.

Contract: Implement shortener using Python's standard library. Inputs satisfy the constraints stated here. Do not mutate the inputs. Use the provided helpers where present; they represent earlier steps.

Examples

Input: requests = [["POST", "https://a.example"], ["POST", "https://b.example"], ["POST", "https://a.example"], ["GET", "1"], ["GET", "missing"]]
Expected: ["1", "2", "1", "https://a.example", null]
Input: requests = []
Expected: []
Hint

Maintain forward and reverse maps. Allocate only for a new URL.

Review your understanding

Write a design in Notes: estimate traffic and storage; choose ID allocation, schema and indexes; add caching, replication, expiry, abuse controls, observability, and a failure policy. Compare a globally sequential ID with range allocation or random IDs. Local tests assess this core only, not the architecture.

Explain your reasoning in Notes before opening the worked solution. Passing the local checks completes this exercise; it does not certify production readiness or evaluate your design explanation.
